Issue Nº 01 — Shooting film on purpose

Slow frames, honest grain.

A journal about shooting Fujifilm emulsions through Fujica glass-and-metal cameras — what the cameras actually do in your hands, which of the five stocks on the shelf earns its place in the bag, and what a roll looks like when you let Bogotá's light decide.

In this issue

  • Three Fujicas, honestly compared — the ST605, STX-1 and ST801, and which one to buy first.
  • Field notes — metering in La Candelaria, pushing black & white, and the frame that got away.
  • The five-stock shelf — pick a stock and see exactly what it does to skin, sky and shadow.
  • Contact sheet Nº 04 — nine frames, filterable by mood. Click any frame to inspect it full-size.

Every photograph on this page is credited to its source under each frame in the lightbox view.

Camera coverage

The Fujicas worth your money

Fujica was Fujifilm's camera brand from the 1950s until the early 1980s. Its 35 mm SLRs are the affordable way into the system: mechanical shutters, bright finders, and Fujinon lenses with the EBC multi-coating that made them famous. Three bodies cover almost every budget.

1979 · Fujica X bayonet

Fujica STX-1

The beginner's Fujica. Fully mechanical shutter (batteries only power the meter's LEDs), a match-LED finder you can read at a glance, and the X-mount Fujinon 50 mm f/1.9 that punches far above its price.

MountFujica X bayonet
ShutterMechanical, B + 1/2–1/700 s
MeterTTL, match-LED in finder
Buy it ifYou want one camera that never depends on electronics

1976 · M42 screw mount

Fujica ST605

The M42 workhorse. Because it takes screw-mount lenses, your lens library is enormous and cheap — and the bundled Fujinon 55 mm f/1.8 EBC is one of the sharpest standard lenses of its era.

MountM42 screw mount
ShutterMechanical, B + 1/2–1/700 s
MeterTTL stop-down, needle
Buy it ifYou want the widest, cheapest lens ecosystem

1978 · M42 screw mount

Fujica ST801

The connoisseur's pick, and the first camera ever sold with LED shutter-speed readouts in the finder. A top speed of 1/2000 s, an unusually bright viewfinder, and a split-image screen that makes manual focus genuinely fast.

MountM42 screw mount
ShutterMechanical, B + 1–1/2000 s
MeterTTL, LED display — a world first
Buy it ifYou shoot fast glass wide open in bright Andean sun

Field rule for all three: budget for new light seals and a CLA before your first important roll. Forty-year-old foam is the only unreliable part of these cameras.

Field notes

Notes from the notebook

Short, practical entries written after development — what worked, what didn't, and the setting to use next time. Open any note to read it in full.

Metering La Candelaria at noon Exposure · Bogotá

At 2,600 metres the midday sun is a stop brighter than your instincts say, and La Candelaria's whitewashed walls bounce it everywhere. The STX-1's centre-weighted meter wants to protect the walls and buries faces in shadow.

What works: meter off the shaded side of the street, lock that reading, then recompose. On Fujicolor 200, overexpose by a third of a stop — the film holds the highlights and the shadows open up beautifully in the scan.

Pushing Acros II one stop for night buses B&W · Technique

Neopan 100 Acros II is famously fine-grained, which makes it an odd choice for night work — until you push it. Rated at EI 200 and developed with +15% time, the grain stays tight, reciprocity failure is a non-issue on this stock, and TransMilenio stations turn into clean, graphic compositions of tube light and silhouette.

Watch out: pushed Acros loses shadow detail fast. Expose for the mid-tones and let the blacks go black — that's the look anyway.

Velvia in the mountains: worth the discipline Slide film · Landscape

Velvia 50 forgives nothing: half a stop of error is visible. But on a clear morning above the páramo, no other stock on the shelf renders that green-on-green hillside with the same saturation. Bracket in third-stops, use a polariser sparingly (Velvia skies go navy fast), and write every exposure down — you will not remember which frame was which.

Verdict: one roll per trip, reserved for the two hours after sunrise. Everything else belongs to the forgiving stocks.

The frame that got away — and why film shooters keep a notebook Process

Frame 23 of a Fujifilm 400 roll: a portrait in perfect window light, except the notebook says “f/2, guessed focus.” It shows. The notebook is not nostalgia — it is the only EXIF film will ever give you. Camera, lens, aperture, shutter, stock, and one line about the light, for every frame you care about.

Community prompt

This month: “One street, one roll”

November 2026 prompt

Walk one street. Shoot one roll. Publish the whole contact sheet.

Pick a single street — yours, or one you have never walked with a camera. Load one roll of any stock from the shelf, walk the street end to end, and finish the roll before you leave. Then share the complete contact sheet, not just the keepers. The near-misses are the point: they show how you see.

Share your sheet wherever you already post your work and tag it with your street and stock. This page doesn't host a gallery — your photos stay yours, on your own channels.

Before you go — the one-roll checklist

  • One street chosen, end to end, on the map
  • One roll loaded — and the ISO dial actually set to match it
  • Notebook and pencil in the pocket (your only EXIF)
  • Spare battery for the meter, even on a mechanical body
  • A turnaround point and a coffee stop planned at the far end
  • Lab drop-off (or dev tank) booked before the roll is finished
  • Contact sheet scanned whole — no cropping the story first

Your browser

Email
